title: My first library card
description: A library card is a small card with a big power: it lets you borrow books, take them home, and swap them for new ones when you are done. Here is how getting your first card works.

body.heading: A card that opens a building full of books
paragraphs: A library is a place where books live so that everyone can read them. You do not buy the books. You borrow them, read them at home, and bring them back so someone else can read them next.
Your library card is how the library knows which books are with you. It has your name on it, and it is yours to look after, like a key to the whole building.

body.heading: Getting your card
paragraphs: A grown-up comes with you to the library desk. You give your name, and soon you get your very own card. The librarian can show you where the children's books are and how many you can borrow at one time.
Pick your first book slowly. Smell it, peek at the pictures, read the first page. When you find one that makes you want to turn the page, that is your book.

body.heading: Bring them back, get more
paragraphs: Books must come back by their due date so other children can borrow them too. Bringing them back on time is part of the deal — and it means you get to choose a whole new pile.
Some children keep a list of every book they borrow. By the end of the year, the list can be longer than they are tall.

takeaway: A library card lets you borrow books for free and swap them for new ones — look after your card, and bring your books back on time.
ageGuidance: Ages 4–8, with a grown-up's help to sign up and visit the library.

supervision: A grown-up must go with the child to sign up for the card and stays with them during library visits.
safetyNotes: Carry books in a bag so they do not get wet or bent.
Keep your library card in a safe place at home, and never share your card number with strangers.
screenFreeExtension: At home, build a tiny library corner with a cushion and your borrowed books, and read one together every night until swap day.
